title: What drives McCoy after second big crash in 13 months?
description: After he injured his back in his second big crash in 13 months, Gary McCoy speaks to the BBC Bikes podcast about his recovery and drive to return to racing.
fullText:
When Gary McCoy slid off his bike at the Isle of Man TT in June, he had two seconds to process what was about to happen.

"'Oh no, not again.' I knew what was coming," he recalled.

The Northern Ireland road racer ended up in hospital with five broken vertebrae in his back, one of which was crushed, and a broken shoulder blade.

Just 13 months earlier, McCoy had another big crash at the North West 200 which left him with serious injuries.

On that occasion, a following rider crashed into McCoy from behind approaching Mill Road roundabout and he was left with a bleed in the brain, a punctured lung and 22 broken bones.

Yet, despite an extensive list of injuries from the two accidents, McCoy plans to get back on the bike and hit the roads again next year.

Speaking to the BBC Bikes podcast, McCoy says he was in "disbelief" after his accident at the Isle of Man TT, and says he was "very, very lucky", but the thought of competing again is not only driving on his recovery, but also his drive to get back to work.

"Whenever you want something bad enough you sort of look by it all, and it keeps you going forward," he said.

"But motorbikes is driving me on, motorbikes is driving me on to get fitter and get better, get back to work, get back to racing.

"If you didn't know motorbikes, you would have no drive. I don't think so. I don't think so. It's driving me on at the minute and long may it last."

McCoy 'awaiting results of scan on vertebrae injuries'

McCoy grew up watching road racing right across Ireland with his family, but it wasn't until he was 21 that he started competing.

He made his North West 200 debut in 2022, when he was the best newcomer, and had several top 10 finishes at the international road race.

After he recovered from his 2025 North West 200 accident, the 27-year-old was primed to make his TT debut for the family-run MadBros team in June, and things had started well.

McCoy had shown impressive form in qualifying as a newcomer but an accident in damp conditions in the opening Supersport race brought his TT debut to a sudden halt.

"Prior to the crash, everything was absolutely amazing. It was the best thing I've ever done," McCoy added.

"It's all I've ever wanted to do from when I was three or four years of age.

"So, after twenty seven years of wanting to do it, and finally getting to do it, it was unbelievable."

On his crash, which happened at the Kerrowmoar section of the 37.73-mile circuit on the third lap of the race, McCoy was still looking at the positives.

"We were just caught out in the damp patch and chatting to a few others, even Michael Dunlap said to the boys he had a wee moment down through it, and Paul Jordan had a wee moment through it.

"A few top boys were having moments, you know, so it's just unfortunate that a newcomer had to get caught out and that is what it is."

McCoy has two young children and a wife, Leana, and admits that road racing is "a very selfish sport".

He admits Leana would be happy if he stayed away from the bike and there is a lot of pressure on her, but she is supportive of him racing.

McCoy says he moved back in with his mum and dad for three months after his 2025 crash as Leana was dealing with a newborn, and says she is a "strong woman".

"You just think it is never going to be you in that situation," McCoy said about the dangers of the sport."

"All I wanted to do was race motorbikes and I'm doing it.

"I can't really explain it any more than that. It's all I've ever wanted. So I'm doing it and I'm not going to give up on it."

McCoy says his full focus is on returning to the North West 200 and Isle of Man TT, where he wants to be progressing.

For the TT in particular, the Cookstown rider said he "can't describe the feeling" of getting ready to set off down Bray Hill for the opening laps.

"Until you actually experience it and until you actually experience it and do the Isle of Man TT, you can't really explain what it means or how it feels.

Listen to the BBC Bikes podcast with Gary McCoy and Stephen Watson on BBC Sounds.

title: Garcia v Benn - all you need to know
description: All you need to know about Ryan Garcia's WBC welterweight title defence against Conor Benn in Las Vegas on Saturday night.
fullText:
Conor Benn will attempt to emulate his father Nigel by winning a world title when he faces WBC welterweight champion Ryan Garcia in Las Vegas on Saturday.

After a blockbuster 2025, in which Benn lost to Chris Eubank Jr before beating his bitter rival in the middleweight rematch, the 29-year-old returns to welterweight in pursuit of world honours.

American Garcia won the WBC belt in February with a hard-fought unanimous decision victory over Mario Barrios.

The 28-year-old, who has a record of 25 wins, two defeats and one no-contest, has home advantage with the bout taking place at Vegas' T-Mobile Arena.

Will Garcia come through his first defence successfully? Or can Benn spring a surprise?

Here is all you need to know about Garcia v Benn.

Live text commentary on the BBC Sport website and app will begin at 03:00 BST on Sunday, 13 September.

Garcia and Benn are not scheduled to make their ringwalks before 04:00.

All timings are estimated and subject to change.

Ryan Garcia (c) v Conor Benn - WBC welterweight world title

Jai Opetaia (c) v Noel Mikaelian - Zuffa cruiserweight title

Damazion Vanhouter v Raphael Akpejiori - heavyweight

Mark Magsayo v Andres Cortes - lightweight

Garcia won 15 national amateur titles before turning professional in 2016 and earning a first-round TKO victory on his debut.

He began his career as a lightweight but also featured at super-featherweight as he stitched together a 20-fight win streak.

Garcia beat Briton Luke Campbell by seventh-round TKO to win the interim WBC lightweight title.

His first career loss came in his 24th bout when he was stopped in round seven by fellow American Gervonta Davis.

In 2024, Garcia was handed a shot at WBC light-welterweight champion Devin Haney but he missed weight and was not eligible to claim the belt after picking up a decision victory.

That result was later overturned to a no-contest; Garcia was also handed a one-year suspension after failing a drugs test.

Garcia lost to Rolly Romero on his return in May 2025 but bounced back with a decision win over Barrios in February to claim his first world title.

Like Garcia, Benn turned professional in 2016 and enjoyed a similarly stunning start to his career, winning his first 23 fights.

In 2023, he was also suspended from boxing for failing two voluntary drugs tests.

His ban was lifted by the National Anti-Doping Panel, although he remained suspended by the UK Anti-Doping Agency (Ukad) and was unable to fight in the UK.

He fought twice in the United States - beating Rodolfo Orozco and Peter Dobson - before his ban was eventually lifted following a two-year battle with Ukad and the British Boxing Board of Control (BBBofC).

Benn's first fight back in the UK ended in defeat against Eubank in April 2025, but he avenged what remains his sole career loss seven months later.

Garcia makes the first defence of his WBC welterweight title.

It is the first time Benn, who is ranked number one by the WBC, will compete for a world title.

Teofimo Lopez holds the WBA belt, with Liam Paro in possession of the IBF title and Devin Haney reigning as WBO champion.

title: Pereira expects UFC rematch with Gane to happen
description: UFC star Alex Pereira insists the fight that makes the most sense for him is a rematch against Ciryl Gane.
fullText:
Alex Pereira has insisted he wants to fight Ciryl Gane next after being knocked out by the Frenchman in their interim heavyweight UFC title fight last June.

Pereira, 39, was stopped by Gane in his bid to become the first three-weight champion in the UFC.

Speaking on social media, Pereira said that after a period of rest, he expected to get a rematch with the 36-year-old.

"I'm seeing many opinions but I think the fight that makes sense is Ciryl Gane," he said.

"That's the fight. I'm going to work on that and from what I'm seeing, it's something that's going to happen.

"How the last fight [ended], there were illegal shots. I think now with another opportunity I can come back and show what I can do, what I can achieve, which is the third belt.

"I'm very excited for that and I'll work for that."

Gane should fight UFC champion Tom Aspinall in what would be an undisputed contest next, but the Briton is still recovering from eye injuries sustained in his own fight against Gane almost a year ago.

Aspinall's return date is unknown but he has been cleared to return to training and insisted he has no plans to leave the UFC or retire.

Should Aspinall be forced to sit out the rest of 2026, Gane may well take another bout in his absence.

How bullying led Britain's Campbell to the UFC

Pereira was unhappy with Gane's tactics in their fight, suggesting several of his heaviest blows were illegal strikes to the back of his head, something his opponent denied.

Gane is in his second spell as interim heavyweight champion and has twice been beaten in fights for the full title.

Brazil's Pereira has been UFC champion at middleweight and light-heavyweight and achieved that feat in just seven fights, the fastest run to two-division champion status in UFC history.

Michael 'Venom' Page has been removed from the UFC rankings after fighting out his contract at UFC Paris on Saturday.

The Briton's lacklustre decision victory over Nursulton Ruziboev was booed by fans inside Accor Arena, with Page landing just 12 significant strikes through three rounds.

Page said he hoped to reach a new deal with the UFC but American journalist John Morgan, external confirmed media were instructed to remove him from their ranking considerations, an indicator he is not renewing with the MMA promotion.

The 39-year-old holds a 5-1 record in the UFC, but has failed to produce the eye-catching knockout performances he is known for.

Posting on his Instagram on Monday, Page gave little away about his immediate future.

"Thank you Paris for having me. I'm grateful for the support you gave me," he said.

"Stepping in the cage is a privilege I do not take for granted and I look forward to bigger challenges."

title: 'Problems run deeper' - Coady on Leicester crisis
description: Former Leicester City defender Conor Coady says the problems at his old club "have got to run deeper" than the manager and players.
fullText:
Former Leicester City defender Conor Coady believes the problems at his old club "have got to run deeper" than the manager and players after their difficult start to life in League One.

The former England international revealed he could feel the decline during his two-season spell in the East Midlands.

Leicester are 18th with five points from their opening five matches and were beaten 4-0 at home by Oxford United on Saturday.

Speaking on BBC Radio 5 Live's Monday Night Club, Coady said the club had been "in transition too long" following three relegations in the past four seasons.

"There's got to be something deep down that's wrong here because it's been going on for too many years," he added.

"Everyone will sit there and go 'the players aren't good enough'. They haven't been good enough. I was there, I felt it, I wasn't good enough when I was there.

"But there's got to be a deeper issue."

Latest Leicester news, analysis and fan views

Listen to Leicester City content on BBC Sounds

Coady joined the Foxes for a reported £8.5m in 2023 following eight years with Wolves but left for Wrexham after two seasons.

He believes Leicester have lost the identity that once made them one of the most difficult sides to face at King Power Stadium and led to the famous Premier League title in 2016 and the FA Cup win in 2021.

Recalling teams containing the likes of Jamie Vardy, James Maddison, Youri Tielemans, Wilfred Ndidi, Wes Morgan and Robert Huth, he added: "It was one of the hardest games you were going to have in a season.

"I just feel like that identity has been lost over the years. I was part of that team when we lost that identity."

Last season, Leicester City owner Khun Aiyawatt 'Top' Srivaddhanaprabha told BBC Sport he shouldered the blame for the club's decline - and he has since put the club on the market with an asking price of more than £200m.

Observer football journalist Rory Smith questioned Leicester's recent managerial appointments and whether there is a clear long-term strategy at the club.

He pointed to the differing styles of Leicester's recent managers and said it "doesn't suggest there's any real strategy" or an "overarching belief" from the ownership about what the club should be.

Smith also believes expectations will make patience difficult, with Leicester regarded as one of the biggest clubs in League One.

"They should have the quality to be relatively competitive within League One regardless," he said.

'That's a sackable performance' - what next for Martin at Leicester?

Oxford loss 'solely down to the players' - Souttar

Coady believes Leicester did make progress over the summer by refreshing the squad and giving opportunities to younger players.

But he said the appointment of Russell Martin requires patience because of the time needed to implement his style of football.

"They've decided to bring Russell in, so you decide to tie your flag to the mast and go, 'right, we are going to go with this'," Coady said.

"If they're going to make a decision after four or five games, there was no point in bringing Russell in because that's not the sort of manager he is."

Former Blackburn Rovers striker Chris Sutton believes Martin's reputation for possession-based football could make his position increasingly difficult if results do not improve.

"There is this perception now which is following him around of his teams just being purely possession-based and all about keeping the ball and not having any thrust or cutting edge," Sutton said.

"The job he's gone into at Leicester, because of the expectation this season, is for them to bounce straight back."

Smith argued Martin's reputation could also mean supporters are less willing to give him time, despite his previous success in guiding Southampton to promotion from the Championship.

Sutton agreed the criticism of Martin following his short spell at Rangers had not always been fair, but said Leicester's ambitions leave little room for a slow start.

"He needs a result or two quickly to turn the tide," Sutton added.

"Leicester fans expect the team to go up, and that's his biggest problem."

title: Como renew striker's contract after cancer diagnosis
description: Italian club Como renew the contract of forward Roberta Picchi after she is diagnosed with breast cancer.
fullText:
Como have extended the contract of their forward Roberta Picchi after she was diagnosed with breast cancer.

The Italian club, who will make their women's Serie A debut this season, said they extended Picchi's contract until the end of the 2027-28 season as part of their "continued commitment" to the player.

The 34-year-old Italian is set to begin cancer treatment and will be supported by Como's medical team, who will work with the ​specialists overseeing her care.

"Everyone at Como ​1907 is alongside Roberta and will give her and her family all the ​support they need during the ​months ahead," the club said in a statement.

"At this time, we ask that Roberta's privacy is respected as she focuses on her treatment ​and recovery."

Picchi was part of the Como side that finished 11 points clear of Lumezzane as they claimed the Serie B title last season to earn their first promotion to the top division of Italian women's football.

"Nothing ​should ever be taken for ​granted, ⁠and I feel fortunate," Picchi wrote on social media.

"It's time to play my match, but ⁠I'll ​be back even ​more determined."

Como, managed by Selena Mazzantini, begin their season against AC Milan on 26 September.

Olympic long jump champion Tara Davis-Woodhall has decided to end her 2026 season after suffering "severe concussion" in a car crash.

The decision means the 27-year-old American will miss this week's World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Hungary.

"This one hurts. I'm sad, disappointed and just hurt by all of it," wrote Davis-Woodhall on social media., external "I know this has to be part of my story.

Davis-Woodhall won long jump gold at the 2024 Olympics in Paris, before topping the podium at the Worlds in Tokyo a year later.

She was involved in a "very scary" head-on collision in August when she was on her way to training.

Afterwards, she said her injuries were not life-threatening but that both cars, which were going at about 20mph, were written off.

title: No goals but Emery knows Villa's forwards need time
description: Aston Villa have not scored in their opening three Premier League games - how will manager Unai Emery find their attacking edge?
fullText:
It is a new era - but Aston Villa have been here before.

No goals in their first three Premier League games, with one shot on target, has followed a summer of change.

They open their second Champions League campaign under Unai Emery at Club Brugge on Tuesday aiming to ignite the season.

Villa took five games to score their first top-flight goal last season before ending the campaign triumphant, winning the Europa League in Istanbul.

Since then, six of the starting XI from that victory have departed Villa Park, leaving them rebuilding their forward line.

Record £65m buy Nicolas Jackson has replaced Ollie Watkins, while Johan Manzambi, Ibrahim Mbaye and Alejandro Garnacho have arrived following Morgan Rogers' £117m move to Chelsea.

Emery has revamped Villa before, but can he find their new attacking edge?

Watch highlights of every Champions League game from 22:00 on Wednesday on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app. 

There will also be a Champions League Match of the Day on BBC One on Wednesday, from 22:40 to 00:00. 

This week there will also be be a highlights show on Thursday on BBC Two at 22:30 with highlights from Thursday's matches dropping at 22:00.

Watkins' departure to Al-Hilal - which lurched between acrimonious and emotional - has left Villa without their best attacking outlet.

Despite just one goal in his first 13 top-flight games last season he ended with 16 to leave for £51m on 91 Premier League goals, a club record.

Jackson was brought in as Watkins' direct replacement and was a priority signing for Emery having worked with him at Villarreal.

Emery gave the Senegal striker his debut at Estadio de la Ceramica and believes he can rely on him to fill the void Watkins has left.

He has started Villa's past two games, the 1-0 defeat by Arsenal and Saturday's draw at Hull.

Jackson scored 30 goals in 81 appearances for Chelsea and the stats slightly favour England's Watkins, when they both played in the Premier League between 2023 and 2025.

In his first Premier League season the 25-year-old scored 14 goals and assisted five, compared with Watkins' 19 goals and 13 assists.

In 2024-25 Jackson scored 10 goals to Watkins' 16 in 382 fewer minutes. He only had eight fewer shots but his conversion rate of 13.2% was inferior to Watkins' of 19.1%.

Jackson's touches in the box are also lower than Villa's departed striker - 168-231 in 2023-24 and 153-182 in 2024-25.

Yet, Jackson's time at Bayern Munich - helping them win the Bundesliga last season - gave him a 21.1% conversion rate, scoring eight goals in 1,004 minutes of game time.

It is why Emery trusts Jackson, but the unknown is being able to gel a new core of players together, however high their potential.

Emery also has to ensure Mbaye - a £47m arrival from Paris St-Germain on deadline day - and Garnacho can provide Jackson the ammunition.

Between them, Watkins and Rogers scored 46% of Villa's goals in the Premier League last season.

Rogers and Lucas Digne provided 12 assists, with Youri Tielemans adding four and Watkins three.

All four have left, so 18-year-old Mbaye and Chelsea loanee Garnacho will be expected to be the supply line, with Brian Madjo and Tammy Abraham supporting Jackson.

Garnacho has, so far, been kept out by George Hemmings - the 19-year-old is highly rated at Villa Park with Emery calling him "clearly a Premier League player".

But the academy product only had 25 minutes of top-flight football before this season so expectations must be managed.

Argentina winger Garnacho created six big chances, earning four assists, at Chelsea last term but scored just once.

Mbaye created four goals in 10 starts for PSG last season, helping them win Ligue 1, and was an unused substitute at Hull on Saturday. Emery will expect more from both once they are in tune with his demands.

Manzambi, one of the World Cup's breakout stars in the summer, has yet to play for Villa after his move from Freiburg as he recovers from a knee injury.

Emery's messaging is crucial, which is why it will take time for them to develop into the cohesive unit the manager demands.

His meetings can last anywhere between 90 minutes and two hours, which naturally tests players' focus levels, but underlines the amount of detail they need to take on board.

To integrate 10 new players, including Jackson, Mbaye and Garnacho, takes time. It is time Emery usually likes to use carefully - but it something he does not have in the current circumstances.

It is why, when he needed players in January, Douglas Luiz returned on loan from Juventus and Abraham arrived from Besiktas.

Luiz knew Emery's methods and Abraham at least knew the club, although neither deal worked - with Luiz returning to Italy and Emery willing to let Abraham go this summer only for the striker to decide to stay.

Only two summer signings - Jackson and goalkeeper Zion Suzuki - started the draw at Hull and Taylor Harwood-Bellis was left out of the squad, underlining the situation Emery must deal with.

"We must be patient, and we should understand that we are rebuilding the team. Now they must get our way and demands, keeping the same mentality that we built, but with different players," said Emery.

"Now is no time to think two weeks or three weeks forward.

"We must try to focus on each match. The next match is the Champions League and something we can feel excited and motivated to play because we deserve to be there.

"Now it is to compete in Brugge on Tuesday. Then, we are going to think about the next match at home against Nottingham Forest.

"Each match is a lot of information we can have. We are collecting information individually and collectively about the players, about the structure, about the capacity to build the team.

"Saturday was one point. It was not enough, but I am feeling optimistic about how the players are responding."

title: Non-league to Champions League: The Porto boss out to stun Man City
description: Porto boss Francesco Farioli is one of the most highly regarded young managers and on Tuesday he takes charge in the Champions League for the first time.
fullText:
Francesco Farioli is one of the fastest-rising stars in coaching.

The 37-year-old led Porto to the Portuguese title last season and is now preparing to take charge of his first Champions League match as a manager against Manchester City at the Estadio do Dragao on Tuesday.

Leading a team out in Europe's premier club competition might still feel a long time coming for Farioli, who was linked with the vacancies at Chelsea, Liverpool and Rangers last season.

However, Farioli, who began his managerial journey in Turkey in 2021 with Fatih Karagumruk and then Alanyaspor, opted to renew his contract instead and is certain he made the right choice.

"I don't feel I could be in a better place," he told BBC Sport.

"I said at our post-season dinner they have created a problem for me, as I will have to bring the president and directors with me."

Chief among the relationships keeping him at Porto has been the one with club president Andre Villas-Boas, the former Tottenham and Chelsea manager.

Watch highlights of every Champions League game from 22:00 on Wednesday on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app. 

There will also be a Champions League Match of the Day on BBC One on Wednesday, from 22:40 to 00:00. 

This week there will also be be a highlights show on Thursday on BBC Two at 22:30 with highlights from Thursday's matches dropping at 22:00.

Another key figure in his story is current Tottenham boss Roberto de Zerbi, who appointed Farioli - then a former non-league goalkeeper in Italy and blogger on the Wyscout coaching platform - on to his backroom staff at Benevento in 2017 and then took him to Sassuolo.

Initially a goalkeeping coach, he moved into management in Turkey before successful spells at Nice in France and Dutch club Ajax.

His time at Ajax did, though, end in disappointment, with the club missing out on the Eredivisie title on the final day. That came after a turbulent January transfer window, during which he felt they had failed to strengthen sufficiently.

The season before his arrival, Ajax had briefly been involved in a relegation battle.

"I am used to entering uncomfortable situations where there is a lack of direction and things are not in place," Farioli said.

"I was looking for a club with a similar spirit, not for revenge, but one that wanted to put things right."

He said Porto had felt the "same pain" after finishing third before his arrival and shared "the same ambition to do something special".

On meeting Villas-Boas in the Italian city of Como before accepting the job, Farioli was reassured to find the club's vision aligned with his own.

Porto won the Portuguese Super Cup last month and will have designs on causing an upset against Enzo Maresca's City. As former European champions who lifted the trophy under Jose Mourinho in 2004, they possess considerable Champions League pedigree.

It is not just Farioli's rise through the game that has attracted attention. Across spells at Nice, Ajax and now Porto, his teams have developed a distinctive identity built on possession, structure and aggressive pressing.

Porto have started this season with five wins out of five, conceding only one goal in the league.

This is the result of impressive tactical understanding alongside a focus on the human part of coaching individuals.

A fitting example of Farioli tying these two parts of management together was seen in the form of an anonymous questionnaire he gave his players about his tactics, allowing the squad to make suggestions.

Farioli produced teams with the best domestic defensive records while in charge of Nice, Ajax and Porto but this does not come from being a 'defensive coach'.

"One year earlier in Ajax, I was accused of being too offensive," he said. "Now in Porto, I was accused of being too defensive. It's probably not one way or another but it is just about balancing the team."

When asked what contributed to his sides being so strong defensively, he referred to this balance between attack and defence.

"A part that is quite underestimated is the part on the ball," he explained. "You cannot really separate moments. These are phases of the same cycle.

"This defensive record comes a lot also from the way that we attack, the type of structure that we want when attacking and how we prepare ourselves in the moment that we lose the ball. Everything is linked."

Porto look to hold the ball for long periods of the game, remaining stationed closer to the opposition goal.

As they attack, they maintain a solid structure of players behind the ball ready to defend counter-attacks.

Around the Porto player on the ball, team-mates are positioned close enough to apply pressure as soon as the ball is lost too - hoping to regain possession quickly.

And this aggressive pressure is not only seen when Porto lose the ball, also coming into play when opponents look to build out from the back.

Porto press high, at times asking three attackers to stifle the build-up of a back five or six, but they manage to prevent opponents finding their free player, a seemingly impossible task.

"A lot goes with understanding and timing, specific triggers, and the capacity for the players to interpret the moment of the game according to where we are on the pitch and what the opponent is trying to do," he added.

"We spend a lot of work on video, correction and explanation. You need players capable to understand and to put the extra effort. The collaboration between players is key."

Returning to Farioli's intertwined approach of using attacking moments to defend and defensive moments to attack, Porto's press does not just look to force opponent's long.

Instead, they entice them to play into the centre of the pitch before looking to win it back, setting them up nicely to attack the goal against a disorganised defence.

"The way that we approach these moments is something I started in my first experience in Turkey, to apply ideas and implement a method. But again, it's not just about the moment off the ball, it's also about the way to attack.

"Something that we experienced a lot with Roberto de Zerbi was to play with certain distances, to have a team very narrow on the ball. It's a way to facilitate the transition moment and to rebalance when we lose the ball, to avoid counter-attacks.

"I believe that football, and life in general, is made by two principles: entropy, meaning chaos, and negative entropy, the intention to bring order.

"As a coach, I can help the team by bringing more order, a language and maybe some glasses to see the reality and how to see the game in the same way."

With Porto facing City on Tuesday, he has the chance to test his ideas against one of the world's best teams.

title: From match point to US Open exit - lucky loser denied history
description: France's Arthur Gea held match point to become the first lucky loser to reach a Grand Slam quarter-final - three hours later he was out of the US Open.
fullText:
France's Arthur Gea was one point away from being the first lucky loser to reach a Grand Slam quarter-final - but three hours later he was out of the US Open.

Gea, 21, was unable to convert a match point in a third-set tie-break against Dutch opponent Botic van de Zandschulp, then could not serve out victory in the fourth set of a gruelling fourth-round contest.

Van de Zandschulp took full advantage to escape from the jaws of defeat, going on to secure a 3-6 6-7 (0-7) 7-6 (9-7) 7-6 (7-3) 6-4 win after five hours and 13 minutes - the fourth longest match on record at Flushing Meadows.

World number 87 Gea was not ranked high enough for the main draw when the US Open entry list was finalised, meaning he had to go through qualifying instead.

Seeded first, he lost to American Nishesh Basavareddy in the third and final round but earned a reprieve when 2022 finalist Casper Ruud withdrew injured on the eve of the tournament.

Gea made the most of the lifeline by beating Argentina's Juan Manuel Cerundolo, Zachary Svajda of the United States and another American Michael Zheng to reach the last 16.

But he could not find a way past 70th-ranked Van de Zandschulp, who said he had "no clue" how he completed a "crazy comeback".

After becoming the 13th lucky loser to be eliminated in the fourth round of a Slam, Gea will receive $480,000 in prize money - a considerable increase on the $66,000 he thought he was taking home from qualifying.

Gauff's statement win completes stacked US Open line-up

Van de Zandschulp's reward for reaching the second US Open quarter-final of his career is a meeting with German top seed Alexander Zverev.

Zverev, 29, had a rare finish before midnight in New York when he beat Italian 21st seed Luciano Darderi 6-2 6-2 7-6 (7-3) to reach the last eight.

Zverev's previous three matches finished at 1:55am, 2:15am and 1:09am.

"I don't know what to do with myself because it's before midnight - I might go back to the practice courts or go to a bar," Zverev joked.

On whether he wants to play Van de Zandschulp in Wednesday's night session, the French Open champion added: "I will request the night match for sure.

"I've rented this court out from 11pm until 2am for two weeks so I hope they will continue putting me on at [night] time."

Earlier on Monday, Belgium's Alexander Blockx said he was "really close" to retiring injured against Argentina's Francisco Cerundolo before playing on to reach his first major quarter-final.

Blockx, seeded 28th, fought through rib pain to win 6-3 4-6 7-5 7-5, becoming the first Belgian man to make the last eight in New York.

"It was really tough from the beginning of the match. I was struggling a lot, especially while serving. It kept getting worse throughout the match," said 21-year-old Blockx.

"I was really close to retiring, to be honest. I was just hanging in there, but if I would have lost the third set, I think the chances were really high of me retiring.

"I'm glad that I kept on playing."

Presuming he is fit enough, Blockx will play Russian world number 50 Karen Khachanov in the quarter-finals on Wednesday.

Khachanov, 30, fought back to win 7-5 4-6 6-7 (6-8) 6-1 6-4 against 14th seed Learner Tien, ending the American's attempt to put four home men in the quarter-finals for the first time since 1995.

title: England should pick English-based players - Baxter
description: Exeter director of rugby Rob Baxter says England's rules on selecting only home-based players are the right thing for the domestic game.
fullText:
Exeter director of rugby Rob Baxter says England's rules on selecting only home-based players are the right thing for the domestic game.

Former England forward Courtney Lawes has called for overseas-based players to be eligible to be picked for the England side.

The 37-year-old, who has won 105 England caps, returned to the Prem this summer with Sale, having spent two years at French side Brive where he was ineligible to represent his country.

Under England's selection policy, players can only be called up from overseas clubs in exceptional circumstances.

Baxter feels it is important the rules are not changed.

"I just don't think, for the good of the English game, you can do it," he told BBC Sport. "It's not that I don't understand the arguments, I do.

Allow overseas stars to play for England - Lawes

"There's two arguments here, do you just want to make all the best players available to play for England or do you want to build Premiership Rugby as part of how you build the England team?

"If the two go together then you have to have some kind of rules and regulations around where the English players play.

"I always caveat any argument and say selfishly I'm talking about what's good for Exeter Chiefs as well - because what's good for Exeter, and every other Premiership side, is knowing there's a real reason for your best English players to stay in this country.

"If it just comes down to purely finance, then it's a tough, competitive situation for us, and when people just throw it out there that players should be allowed to play anywhere they like, I think you've got to look down at the deeper repercussions of what may actually happen in the English game overall."

Under the rules as they stand, England are unable to call on players such as Toulouse back row Jack Willis - who was voted the best player in France in 2024-25 - as well as Kyle Sinckler, Manu Tuilagi, Billy Vunipola, Lewis Ludlam and former Exeter star Sam Simmonds.

Prem clubs benefit from central payments from the Rugby Football Union (RFU) for their England players, with the national side having a greater say on their management as a result.

England's policy is similar to that of Ireland and New Zealand, while nations such as Scotland, South Africa and Australia do pick players from overseas.

"You can't pick and choose a model just to decide this is what will be good or bad for a country," added Baxter.

"For some countries they're very strict on it and it works really well for them. We've got to decide what we're comfortable with and stick to it."

title: Who will reach Super Bowl? - NFL predictions for 2026 season
description: Who are favourites to reach the Super Bowl and who will be the surprise standouts? BBC's NFL experts make their predictions for the 2026 season - and so can you.
fullText:
The NFL is notoriously difficult to predict and last season was no different.

Seven of the eight division winners were different from 2024, with two of the Super Bowl favourites missing out on the play-offs entirely - the Baltimore Ravens and Kansas City Chiefs.

Two outsiders then made it all the way to the big game, with the Seattle Seahawks beating the New England Patriots for their first NFL championship in 12 years.

So, who will be this season's surprise package? Who will be playing at Super Bowl 61 next February? And who will be the main men?

Here, the BBC's NFL experts make their picks for the 2026 season, which begins this week. Plus you can predict your Super Bowl winner at the bottom of this page.

Rob Staton: I think the NFC will be another battle between the Los Angeles Rams and Seattle Seahawks. I'm going to go with the Rams, simply because only two teams have repeated since the turn of the century. I have them facing the Buffalo Bills. Josh Allen finally gets to the big game.

Hugh Ferris: You could argue that, aside from an underwhelming head coach hire, there's little reason the 2026 Bills will be any different to the recent incarnations. I'm picking them to finally get over the line, though, and reach the Super Bowl, but to lose nonetheless. It's incredibly difficult to choose anyone else rather than the Rams, isn't it?

Haydn Parry: Surely the Bills can convert Allen's talent and make it to the season showpiece? Joe Brady's promotion to head coach might prove to be the missing ingredient. From the NFC, I think the Rams look most likely to have a strong tilt this campaign, and I see them winning it.

Joe Bradshaw: The last time the Super Bowl was at SoFi Stadium in 2022, the Rams won on home territory and they look primed to repeat next February. From the AFC, surely Bills quarterback Allen is overdue a trip to the NFL's biggest game, even if it will ultimately end in defeat.

David Brindle: After losing Bo Nix to injury in last season's play-offs, I expect the Denver Broncos to use that as motivation and at least go one further this season. As for the Rams, it's very difficult to look past the consensus predictions for the Super Bowl.

Ben Collins: Full disclosure, I'd seen the above before writing this so here's some leftfield picks... imagine if it's the Los Angeles Chargers that actually get to play in the Super Bowl in their own stadium, and it's former Rams quarterback Jared Goff that leads Detroit to victory.

Rob Staton: I'm going with Josh Allen. He now has an offensive-minded head coach running the team. Everything will be geared towards him having a big season.

Hugh Ferris: In an attempt to think outside the box, I'm picking Justin Herbert of the Chargers. You might suggest a quarterback in a Jim Harbaugh team isn't likely to get the chance to have an MVP-level season, but the hiring of Mike McDaniel as offensive coordinator might change that.

Haydn Parry: I might be wearing my blue-star goggles here but Dak Prescott has the ability and the weapons to have an outstanding season. Offence was not the Dallas Cowboys' problem last year and it certainly wasn't Prescott's fault that the team failed to deliver. Dallas just need to find a 'D'.

Joe Bradshaw: Buffalo's new head coach Joe Brady has stepped up from offensive coordinator so knows how to get Josh Allen purring. If the Bills make the Super Bowl, their quarterback will be the obvious candidate for his second MVP award.

David Brindle: If it wasn't to be a quarterback, I fancy Jahmyr Gibbs. He's signed a new deal and now has no running back competition at Detroit so expect him to see lots of action on a Lions team who are NFC contenders.

Ben Collins: Cincinnati have remedied their defence and still have a top offence. After twice winning comeback player of the year, quarterback Joe Burrow stays fit long enough to bag the award he really wants as the Bengals make a deep play-off run.

Rob Staton: It could be Joe Brady if he can help Josh Allen reach MVP status, but in order to mix things up I'm going for DeMeco Ryans. The Houston Texans are going to lead on their defence and I think they'll be really strong.

Hugh Ferris: If the Bills reach the Super Bowl, then it stands to reason Joe Brady gets the nod as a first-year head coach, putting to shame people (like me) who called him an underwhelming hire.

Haydn Parry: I have always been a big fan of John Harbaugh. He will start from a comparatively low base in New York with the Giants, but with their passionate fanbase and the enormous potential of Jaxson Dart lift-off could be achieved early.

Joe Bradshaw: There has been such turnover on the NFL's coaching carousel, it has been hard to keep up this off-season. In the face of such instability, I'll opt for Sean McVay as he steers the Rams to their third Super Bowl title.

David Brindle: I'm going for Sean Payton to pick up his second award, 20 years after winning it with New Orleans. With the work done so far and decisions Payton has already made at Denver, this is the year I think it'll be formally recognised.

Ben Collins: After Detroit were hindered by a defensive injury crisis last season, Dan Campbell is rewarded as he gets the Lions roaring again.

Rob Staton: I'd expect Rueben Bain to have an immediate impact in Tampa Bay. Jadarian Price will get opportunities to shine in Seattle. I was a big fan of De'Zhaun Stribling, taken by the San Francisco 49ers. But in terms of pure impact, give me Caleb Downs, the safety in Dallas.

Hugh Ferris: The 49ers have one wide receiver AWOL, another out for the season, and injury question marks over Mike Evans and George Kittle - who's recovering from a torn Achilles - so along with a returning Deebo Samuel, there's a gap for De'Zhaun Stribling to fill.

Haydn Parry: It will be interesting to see how wide receiver Carnell Tate, fourth overall pick by Tennessee, adapts among the big boys. With his versatile skillset, the Titans expect him to contribute right from the off - the pre-draft scout reports highlighted his maturity, intelligence, sure hands and catch radius.

Joe Bradshaw: De'Zhaun Stribling was a surprise selection by the 49ers at the start of the second round but given their annual injury issues, he could be in line for plenty of work this season. Some fine displays in pre-season have only increased the hype.

David Brindle: After Kenneth Walker departed, the Seahawks picked Jadarian Price in the draft. He'll start the season as their lead back, with Zach Charbonnet still recovering from an ACL tear. I expect him to keep that job and become a top running back in the league for many years.

Ben Collins: Sonny Styles' athleticism caught the eye of NFL teams during the pre-draft process. He could have a big impact at linebacker for the Washington Commanders and soon become one of their leaders.

Rob Staton: I'm not suggesting the Las Vegas Raiders are going to go on an improbable run or anything, but Klint Kubiak did an excellent job in Seattle [as offensive coordinator] and should make the transition to head coach with ease. I think this will be the year, finally, that the Raiders show signs of growth.

Hugh Ferris: Here's a surprise: the New York teams won't both be terrible. The Jets' draft and John Harbaugh going to the Giants should mean they could rise to the heady heights of being mediocre.

Haydn Parry: Fernando Mendoza worked wonders at Indiana last year. He probably needs to perform miracles in Las Vegas but it will be fascinating to follow his progress. The lad needs broad shoulders to carry the weight of expectation but the Raiders can hardly do worse than last season.

Joe Bradshaw: Can you call a team with consecutive 11-win seasons a surprise package? Despite great regular seasons, the Los Angeles Chargers have faltered in the play-offs but they are now healthy again and new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel looks a perfect fit for talented quarterback Justin Herbert.

David Brindle: Given they missed the play-offs and went 6-11 last season, if the Cincinnati Bengals can stay healthy - especially quarterback Joe Burrow, who missed most of last season with turf toe - they could reach the Super Bowl and upset the status quo.

Ben Collins: Kevin Stefanski was twice named coach of the year at Cleveland and now has a more stable team at his disposal in Atlanta, led by dual-threat running back Bijan Robinson. If the Falcons can settle on a quarterback, they could finally get back in play-off contention.

Rob Staton: The Cleveland Browns are a shambles. The situation surrounding Deshaun Watson is a mess, and it's frankly incredible he's still in the league. They can no longer rely on Myles Garrett. They seem destined to fail.

Hugh Ferris: I picked the Browns last year and got it wrong. That won't stop me doing it again this year. They're going with Deshaun Watson as their starting quarterback, which will do little other than prove one more time that it might have been the worst trade (and contract) in NFL history.

Haydn Parry: There seems to be a general consensus that the Miami Dolphins are 'in transition' - which is NFL-speak for 'total rebuild'. They are probably in a race to the bottom with the Arizona Cardinals as things stand.

Joe Bradshaw: Iconic edge rusher Myles Garrett has left the Browns and they still have huge questions at quarterback with Deshaun Watson booed by his own fans during pre-season. Their best hope is a top pick in 2027's stacked-looking draft.

David Brindle: Until now, all of the questions have been tough, but this is easy. After a tumultuous off-season where they moved on from Jaylen Waddle and others, the rebuild is under way for the Miami Dolphins and they face a daunting season.

Ben Collins: Although I'm rooting for British tight end Seydou Traore in his rookie year, this could be a long season for the Dolphins. Their roster looks short on talent having also let Tua Tagovailoa and Tyreek Hill go, with Malik Willis entering a season as starting quarterback for the first time.

title: Mourinho, Inter and Champions League: Can he deliver again at Real Madrid?
description: Jose Mourinho begins his second Real Madrid spell in the Champions League against former club Inter Milan, 16 years after winning the trophy with Inter at the Bernabeu. Will he finally deliver European glory in Madrid?
fullText:
There are few more fitting opponents for Jose Mourinho's return to the Champions League as Real Madrid boss than Inter Milan.

Sixteen years ago, Mourinho stood in the Santiago Bernabeu and lifted the trophy after leading Inter to a 2-0 victory over Bayern Munich in the 2010 final.

It was his second Champions League triumph, after Porto in 2004, and the final match of his Inter reign.

Days later, he was appointed Real Madrid manager for his first spell at the club.

Now, after an absence of more than a decade, Mourinho is back in the Bernabeu dugout and Inter are the visitors on Tuesday (20:00 BST).

For Real Madrid, the match provides the first test of whether the manager they returned to can lead them back to Champions League glory.

Watch highlights of every Champions League game from 22:00 on Wednesday on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app. 

There will also be a Champions League Match of the Day on BBC One on Wednesday, from 22:40 to 00:00. 

This week there will also be be a highlights show on Thursday on BBC Two at 22:30 with highlights from Thursday's matches dropping at 22:00.

When Mourinho arrived at Real Madrid in 2010, the brief was clear. He needed to challenge Barcelona, to win La Liga and, above all, deliver the club's 10th European Cup.

He did win trophies. Real lifted the Copa del Rey in 2011 and La Liga in 2012, while Mourinho's side also reached three consecutive Champions League semi-finals.

But they could not get beyond that stage.

Real were beaten by Barcelona in 2011, Bayern Munich on penalties in 2012 and Borussia Dortmund in 2013. Mourinho eventually left in 2013 without delivering the Champions League trophy Real wanted.

But he is adamant his previous spell should not define what happens this time.

"At Real Madrid, I'm going through two different periods," Mourinho said. "I ended working for Real Madrid in 2013... This is a closed chapter. This match against Inter has nothing to do with the past."

Mourinho has returned to a club that endured what he described as a "very complicated season" and where stability is now essential.

"What I've found at Real Madrid is what I've always found here," he said. "The best club in the world.

"Obviously in the Bernabeu, I've won the Champions League, I've lost a Champions League semi-final through penalties, but I've had the best and the worst in this stadium.

"I'm not thinking about this. I think that I'm the coach of Real Madrid and a Champions League game is going to happen."

But he also acknowledged the club needs to rebuild a stable foundation after a difficult campaign.

"Real is Real and at Real Madrid, you have to win," Mourinho added.

That pressure is nothing new to him. His appeal to Real Madrid lies partly in his experience of managing elite dressing rooms and, crucially, knowing what it takes to win the Champions League.

Kylian Mbappe offered a similar assessment when asked whether Mourinho had been brought in to restore authority.

"Mourinho brings his whole career," Mbappe said. "He is a guy who knows how to win, to have a group around him and he knows about giving motivation to the whole group."

This could be year I win Ballon d'Or, says Mbappe

How 'unique' Bellingham is thriving in Mourinho's system

Can Mourinho restore Real Madrid to former glory?

Real's preparations before their first Champions League game of the season have not been perfect.

They lost to Real Betis at the weekend, a result Mourinho believes came despite a strong attacking performance.

"We lost because we have not been able to translate offensive production into goals," he said.

When asked about the loss, Mbappe was keen to not overreact. His injury-time penalty was saved by Real Betis keeper, Alvaro Valles.

"The most important thing is to score goals and that is my responsibility," he said. "We are very relaxed."

The French forward also rejected the idea that Real's two trophyless seasons should create an additional burden for the new Champions League season.

"My experience with Real Madrid says I shouldn't think too long-term because a lot can change," he said.

"I want to think how I can be ready now, to help my team to win the game against Inter Milan and to start the Champions League in a good way."

Mourinho's connection with Inter remains strong.

"I would love to see people from Inter before and after the game," he said.

"But during the game, they won't see me as a friend," he added. "I want Real Madrid to win. This is football's nature."

Mourinho does not believe the match will decide the campaign as there are seven more league-phase games to come, but he knows every point matters.

"Tomorrow is not especially important as it won't decide anything. We have seven games and I think us and Inter will qualify and we might meet again in the future," he said.

"But every point is important and I'm sure a top team like Inter is trying to get points. We will try to win, of course we will," he added.

As Mourinho left the press conference, an Italian journalist stood up and gifted him a small garden sprinkler, wrapped in a bow.

It was to represent the 2010 Champions League semi-final between Inter and Barcelona.

Mourinho's Inter reached the final, despite losing the second leg at Camp Nou. After the final whistle, Mourinho ran on to the pitch to celebrate with his players, and the Camp Nou sprinklers were turned on while Inter were celebrating.

The image of Mourinho celebrating as the sprinklers sprayed across the pitch became iconic, a lasting symbol of his unforgettable 2010 triumph with Inter.

More than a decade on, it is clear the impact he left on the club is still held in high regard by Inter supporters and journalists.

Sixteen years after that triumph, the club that gave him his greatest European night is now the first obstacle in his attempt to create another one.

title: Russell hindered or just Antonelli brilliance? - F1 Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the Italian Grand Prix.
fullText:
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli climbed from 19th on the grid to win the Italian Grand Prix - his home race - in one of the great Formula 1 drives.

Antonelli extended his lead at the top of the drivers' standings to 66 points over team-mate George Russell.

Max Verstappen, in the Red Bull, finished third to complete the podium at Monza.

BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before round 14 of the 2026 season in Madrid, Spain.

Antonelli 'walks over water' for win that will go down in F1 folklore

Why wasn't George Russell given the opportunity by Mercedes to pit under the virtual safety car in the Italian Grand Prix? I know he had the hard tyres on, but as the lead driver on track should he not have been at least given the choice? - Tom

In hindsight, it would be easy to think there would be some controversy around the decisions that were taken when the virtual safety car was called mid-race at the Italian Grand Prix.

In reality, though, there was not any.

At the time, George Russell was leading the race on the hard tyre and Kimi Antonelli was second on the medium, a few laps after the Mercedes drivers had been advised to call off their 'yo-yo' scrapping to allow them to optimise their pace and build a gap to Max Verstappen's Red Bull.

Without a VSC, the question was whether the mediums on Antonelli's car would last to the end - probably not - and what Mercedes would do about that.

With or without the VSC, the race result was up in the air.

The VSC changed the complexion of the race, but Russell, who had fitted hards at the red flag with the express intention of going to the end, said he had given no thought to changing tyres at the time.

"I didn't," he said. "I actually thought the guys behind me were going to stay out as well. But I'm sure the team were quite nervous on the pit wall watching our battle and were probably quite happy to send us on different strategies.

"And of course, when we had Max in the mix as well, from a team perspective, you're covering off both scenarios.

"If either of us were to pit, it was going to be Kimi. And that's why I was just a little bit annoyed with the timing of that VSC because I think it would have been tough for those guys on the medium to have competed with anybody on the hard tyre. But it takes nothing away from Kimi's drive."

At the time, Mercedes' strategy computers were saying staying out was the best option.

Team principal Toto Wolff said: "We didn't know what was the better strategy. At that stage, the system said that the one-stop comes out ahead. That two-stop was coming close to the end, but didn't catch it. That's what the software said."

All of which goes to underline the main takeaway - the sublime quality of Antonelli's drive.

He made remarkable progress up through the field from 19th on the grid, wasting no time in picking off cars in front, minimising any loss from overtaking to his overall race time.

He made this look easy, but as many other drivers proved at Monza on Sunday, overtaking another car of similar performance and immediately pulling away was anything but.

This was a performance for the ages - like Lewis Hamilton in Brazil in 2021, Max Verstappen in Brazil in 2024 or 2025, or Fernando Alonso in Valencia in 2012.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella, who knows a thing or two about this sort of performance having worked with Michael Schumacher and Alonso, said: "While he had a very competitive car, we have to say that he beat a team-mate starting second on the grid.

"It's a very special day, very important for his championship. But for his career and for the fans, motorsport in general, this will be an iconic day. This will be remembered in the years to come."

Is Charles Leclerc's tendency to crash out of races starting to become a problem both for him and Ferrari? - Nathan

Charles Leclerc certainly did not have his best day in Monza on Sunday.

He was arguably too aggressive with Lewis Hamilton at the first chicane on the first lap, forcing his team-mate into the gravel and dropping him to 10th, and crashed out a lap later.

"I wouldn't say that this is the issue," he said. "From lap one to lap two, I had a bit of a difference in power delivery. We'll look into it, but I don't want to comment too much before checking the data and confirming it 100%."

Having said that, does the allegation that Leclerc has a "tendency to crash out of races" stand up?

He has done it twice so far this year - the previous time was in Monaco, when he lost control at a restart on the broken track surface at Anthony Noghes.

But, unless I've missed something, you have to go back nearly three years to the one before that, when he retired with car damage after an incident-packed race at Zandvoort in 2023.

In that period, for comparison, Hamilton has done the same thing four times - Brazil and Netherlands last year, Austin in 2024 and Qatar in 2023.

Ferrari clearly have some things to sort out, however, in terms of their operations and general approach.

Hamilton is not happy about the way the team have effectively disregarded his - albeit slim - title hopes this year in favour of driver equality, and he said after dropping more points to Antonelli on Sunday that it was "far too late for those decisions to come".

The incident between Leclerc and Hamilton on lap one took place in the context of Hamilton saying after qualifying they had to "work as a team to try and topple" Mercedes.

Leclerc said of the first-corner incident: "I don't really know who is forcing that narrative that we are one against the other. I mean, honestly, Zandvoort there was way too many talks already.

"Here it's true, though, that we went too far. Lewis in Turn One, then Turn Two, I tried to do the tightest corner possible, but that was just not enough and doing it here is not good."

Hamilton was not impressed by the suggestion he had done anything wrong at Turn One.

When those remarks were put to Hamilton, he said: "He said what? I was ahead in Turn Two. By the ethics, I was ahead. There was no 'we' in it."

He added: "I don't race dirty. I've always raced clean and fairly and always left space."

Team boss Frederic Vasseur, who said he would talk to the drivers before discussing this in the media, has some smoothing out to do before this weekend's race in Madrid.

Listen - Italian GP Review: History at Monza!

Aston Martin have had their major upgrades but were right at the back of the grid again in Monza. Have the upgrades just failed? - Colin

Aston Martin had a major car upgrade in Hungary two races ago, and a "spec two" Honda engine at the race before Italy in Zandvoort, on either side of the summer break.

There is no question the car upgrade worked. What was effectively an all-new car, apart from the rear suspension and gearbox, cut lap times by about two seconds.

Fernando Alonso made it into the second part of qualifying for the first time all year in Hungary, and drove an outstanding race to finish ninth on merit in the Netherlands, on a one-stop strategy, holding at arm's length the faster Alpine of Pierre Gasly and Racing Bull of Yuki Tsunoda in the final stint.

More upgrades are expected, in the form of a weight reduction around the gearbox, for either Madrid this weekend or Azerbaijan.

The Honda engine upgrade that made its debut in Zandvoort has been less impressive, which is why Aston Martin found themselves at the back again on the power-sensitive Monza track.

Trackside general manager and chief engineer Shintaro Orihara says Honda "observed a step forward in terms of performance from our metrics".

But if there has been one, it is small. Drivability of the spec two in Zandvoort was noticeably worse, too, although it had made a step forward in Italy.

The Aston Martin car seems to be a midfield-level chassis now, somewhere around the borderline of getting into the final part of qualifying, depending on circuit layout, if it had a competitive engine.

And on the chassis side, the team have a sense of direction that gives them confidence they can make another step next season.

With Honda, which still has comfortably the worst engine in F1, the upgrade has been less reassuring.

What is the new Madring circuit in Spain like in terms of power compared to all the previously visited circuits? Who is it expected to suit most of all? - Andrew

The Madrid circuit which makes its debut this weekend has been built from scratch.

The circuit layout has lots of corners, and it is expected to have a low power sensitivity, around the level of Zandvoort.

Medium-speed corners predominate. And overtaking is expected to be difficult - again, like Zandvoort, or even Hungary.

Given Lando Norris took dominant wins in the Netherlands and Hungary, some teams believe McLaren might be favourites heading into this weekend, but McLaren themselves are not so sure.

Hungary and Zandvoort have long-duration corners, where the McLaren excels. But the Madring corners are generally short duration, the exception being the long, banked Monumental, which is expected to be flat out.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said after the race in Monza on Sunday: "We still think that tracks like Baku and Madrid, where you have to be very precise with the trajectory, short corners, maybe they don't play to the best of our car.

"Yet, we have to say that in Zandvoort and Hungary we were in position to win races and here, while we were not, we know that it's a special race.

"Drag will be less important in Madrid. There is a much higher density of corners. We will definitely give it a go."

New tracks always throw up surprises. So, in short, while one can speculate about car and circuit characteristics all one wants, no one will actually know until qualifying on Saturday.

title: Newcastle were 'preparing for months' for Howe departure
description: Newcastle United sporting director Ross Wilson says the club were preparing for former head coach Eddie Howe's departure for up to nine months.
fullText:
Newcastle United sporting director Ross Wilson says the club were preparing for former head coach Eddie Howe's departure for up to nine months.

Although Howe had originally intended to carry on this season, the drained manager decided to step down in July because he felt it was in the best interests of all parties for him to take a break.

It was a summer of huge change as several key players departed, but Newcastle did not envisage Howe leaving when he did following nearly five years in charge.

However, Wilson is adamant the Englishman's exit was not "chaotic" or "painful" because the club had a contingency plan in place, which led to the appointment of Matthias Jaissle.

"We always knew where we were going to go," Wilson said. "That doesn't mean we were always going to Matthias, but he was always part of our planning.

"Part of our responsibility as leaders of the club is to be prepared and Eddie is an exceptionally talented coach.

"That means he was probably going to do something else at some point so we had to be prepared for that."

Newcastle spoke to multiple candidates, but Wilson said Jaissle emerged as their first-choice to replace a "legend of the club".

The Scot, who was appointed in October, said he had "been planning for a managerial change for eight or nine of those months" in the background.

Newcastle's hierarchy always knew they wanted Howe's eventual successor to build on the foundations he put in place with an aggressive, high-pressing playing style.

Jaissle also had a history of developing younger players, particularly during his previous spell at Red Bull Salzburg, which aligned with Newcastle's strategy of targeting signings aged 24 and under.

Following Wilson's first meeting with Jaissle, who joined from Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli, Newcastle chief executive David Hopkinson told him he sounded "really excited about this one".

"I didn't deliberately go on the phone to do that," Wilson said. "But I remember saying 'you're probably right. I think this is it'."

Jaissle remains unbeaten in his first four games in charge of Newcastle in all competitions.

However, only three of the club's eight summer signings - Lukas Hornicek, Amar Dedic and Nico Gonzalez - started in the 2-2 draw against Bournemouth.

It felt like a reminder of the time it will take some of the new arrivals to bed in during what Jaissle has repeatedly called a "transition phase".

Newcastle have forecast a range of financial scenarios, depending on where the club finish this season, but Wilson maintained the German has not been set a specific target for the campaign.

Hopkinson, though, reiterated that Newcastle's ultimate ambition is to "consistently and credibly compete" for the top honours in the long run.

After entering into a Uefa settlement, following a breach of the European football governing body's financial rules, Hopkinson stressed Newcastle needed to be compliant with the game's regulations to do so.

The Magpies have set out to boost revenues by 50% between now and 2030 - mainly through sponsorship deals - but trading players will remain a key part of the club's strategy in order to reinvest.

"We want to have players here who are on a journey with us," Wilson said.

"Equally, if some of those players' journeys go at rapid speed, they might go somewhere else but, of course, that's normal. That's part of football."

Although Newcastle had prepared for the departures of Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali, to Barcelona and Tottenham Hotspur respectively, the club had never planned to lose talisman Bruno Guimaraes.

Newcastle also had to readjust during the window after top targets Victor Munoz and Johan Manzambi joined Liverpool and Aston Villa respectively.

However, aside from Guimaraes going to Arsenal, Wilson claimed "everything else that happened during the window was part of the plan".

"That does not mean that every single player [who signed] was the number one name on our list, but that is never the case in any transfer window," he said.

"Clearly we were disappointed a couple of times but, again, that's normal.

"No club goes into the window and reaches the end getting every target they set out to get. If they say they did, it is a lie."

title: How Alcaraz can single-handedly end American dreams
description: Three Americans have the chance to become the first home US Open men's champion since 2003. But Carlos Alcaraz stands in the way.
fullText:
It could be Carlos Alcaraz versus the United States over the next few days.

The Spanish superstar's popularity at the US Open might be severely tested if he single-handedly prevents an American having the chance to become the first home men's singles champion in 23 years.

Three American players - Ben Shelton, Frances Tiafoe and Alex Michelsen - remain in the draw. All three are in the same half as Alcaraz.

On Tuesday, the defending champion takes on eighth seed Ben Shelton in the quarter-finals.

If the seven-time major winner comes through that blockbuster clash, he will face either Frances Tiafoe or Alex Michelsen in the semi-finals.

And if Alcaraz wins again to reach the Flushing Meadows final, the host nation's long wait for somebody to finally follow in Andy Roddick's 2003 footsteps continues.

Alcaraz says he expects to be facing 24,000 New Yorkers on Arthur Ashe Stadium as well as Shelton, who is looking to reach his second US Open semi-final.

"I think he [will] use the crowd, the people behind him, especially when he's playing here at home," said Alcaraz.

If Ashe can help 23-year-old Shelton earn his first career win over Alcaraz, there is guaranteed to be an American player in the final.

Home stars reaching the men's semi-finals has not been uncommon this century, but only Taylor Fritz has reached the final - two years ago when he lost to Jannik Sinner - since Roddick was beaten by Roger Federer in the 2006 final.

Tiafoe, who is seeded 11th, lost to Fritz in another all-American semi-final and was also eliminated by Alcaraz at the same stage in 2022.

Now the 28-year-old is aiming for a third opportunity to reach his first Grand Slam final.

Tiafoe reached the Cincinnati final last month and, thriving off the energy of the New York crowd, has maintained his momentum.

On what it is like to receive such support, he said: "It's an out-of-body experience, no question. No real explaining that type of feeling.

"It's like you're not even touching the ground at one point. Energy is so high, and it seems like the level of play matches that."

While Tiafoe is one of the sport's great entertainers, 22-year-old Michelsen is more understated.

The world number 46 admits he has been happy to fly "under the radar" at Flushing Meadows while the likes of Tiafoe, Shelton, Fritz and Tommy Paul soak up the attention.

But earning a place in a Grand Slam quarter-final for the first time, and not dropping a set on his way, means Michelsen will find himself under the spotlight on Ashe.

"First, second, third rounds, all matches I'm feeling nerves. It's a human experience," he said.

"But it's just about going out there and managing them to the best of my ability. I feel like I've done that very well."

Six men and women from the United States have reached the last eight at Flushing Meadows this year - the highest tally since 2002 - with three players in each draw.

Along with Tiafoe or Michelsen in the men's, the home fans know they are guaranteed to see at least one American reach the women's semi-finals.

Third seed Jessica Pegula, who is yet to land a major title despite her consistency on the WTA Tour, meets Emma Navarro in another all-American clash on Tuesday.

Coco Gauff - who sits on the other side of the draw - can join Pegula or Navarro by beating Russian fifth seed Mirra Andreeva on Wednesday.

But, unlike the men, there is not a long American drought on the women's side.

Gauff, 22, is looking to win the women's title for the second time, having lifted the trophy in 2023 as a teenager to fulfil the promise she had already long shown.

Pegula, 31, was a beaten finalist in 2024 when she lost to Aryna Sabalenka, who also beat Navarro in the semi-finals that year.

Navarro, 25, has not reached the same stage of a major since, but is rediscovering her best form after stepping back from the tour earlier this season because of health issues.

After beating Russian 21st seed Anna Kalinskaya on Ashe in the last 16, Navarro joked she should have tried getting the home fans on her side before facing Pegula.

"I should have talked to the crowd a little, asking them to come back and cheer me on for that match. I'm definitely going to need them," she said.

title: Architect of UK’s AI policy quits after Anthropic conflict of interest concerns
description:
Matt Clifford forced to stand down amid disquiet from senior MPs over his new full-time job at AI company 
The chair of the UK government’s “moonshot” science and technology research unit has been forced to stand down after taking a job with the San Francisco AI firm Anthropic, in a move senior MPs called a “clear conflict of interest”.
Matt Clifford announced last week that he was taking a full-time job working for the company behind the Claude chatbot, “leading its engagement” with governments outside the US – including the UK. But he retained his leadership at the UK’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency (Aria), which funds frontier science and tech projects.
